articles.title: Novo Nordisk modernizes manufacturing process documents with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
articles.content: Novo Nordisk (Novo) is one of the world’s leading global pharmaceutical companies, manufacturing medicines for chronic diseases such as diabetes and obesity, and delivering them to patients across many countries. Behind every product lies a manufacturing network that adheres to strict quality requirements. Every quality-relevant process step must be described, controlled, and validated through formal documentation. Keeping this documentation current and accurate is a core responsibility of the Manufacturing Technology team within the Tablet area, a responsibility that spans a large and diverse portfolio of controlled documents, including standard operating procedures, work instructions, forms, and training materials, across the global organization. Managing this portfolio presents significant challenges. Document updates are frequent, driven by regulatory changes, process improvements, equipment modifications, and audit findings. Each update demands careful review, structured approval workflows, and timely communication to all affected stakeholders. With thousands of active documents spread across multiple divisions, departments, and product programs, tracking which documents are due for revision, pending approval, or require immediate attention becomes increasingly complex. Much of this oversight currently relies on manual processes and fragmented tracking methods such as spreadsheets or disconnected systems. These methods are time-consuming, error-prone, and difficult to scale. The result is a risk of outdated documentation remaining in circulation, delayed updates, and critical gaps in compliance visibility. Beyond document management, there is a deeper knowledge challenge. Valuable manufacturing knowledge is distributed across many controlled documents, versions, sites, and product programs. Finding the right answer at the right time often depends on experienced individuals knowing where to look. This dependency on tribal knowledge creates bottlenecks that slow down decision-making and, ultimately, impact how quickly life-saving medicines reach patients. To address these challenges, the Manufacturing Technology team within the Tablet area has embarked on developing an intelligent support system powered by agentic AI, deployed on AWS. The goal is to reduce lead times, improve documentation visibility, and make critical manufacturing knowledge more accessible, ultimately helping the organization move faster and serve more patients around the world. This post dives deep into the architecture and the key design decisions made to meet the high standards of accuracy and traceability required in a regulated pharmaceutical environment. The solution helped subject-matter experts (SMEs) complete work that used to take hours or days in minutes. We also describe an AI process-intelligence assistant that can answer complex process questions with grounded, cited responses. The solution is built around a GraphRAG architecture, combining a knowledge graph with hybrid search to retrieve the most relevant and contextually accurate information. AI agents, built on a managed agent framework, coordinate the retrieval and response process end-to-end. A guided mode helps clarify ambiguous questions before a search is initiated, helping make responses more precise and defensible. The challenge Teams supporting manufacturing repeatedly answer variations of the same question: what does the process require, for this site, this product, and this equipment? Answering well requires four things at once: The right document out of a large corpus. The right version and lifecycle state (approved and effective, not draft or obsolete). The right scope (it actually applies to the site, product generation, and equipment). The relationships (which documents reference which, and what a change would impact). articles.title: A shared signal for humans and robots: Flexible display uses both color and near-infrared to communicate
articles.content: A joint research team from the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST) and Yonsei University has developed a flexible display that can communicate information to both humans and robots. Human workers can interpret information through visible color changes, while robots can detect near-infrared patterns invisible to the human eye. The technology could serve as an "electronic tag" attached to products or equipment, allowing humans and robots to monitor work status using the same display.

articles.title: With Qwen4-Max, Alibaba puts the open source jacket back on the hanger
articles.content: Alibaba has officially unveiled Qwen4-Max, the first model in its next-generation Qwen4 family, with a focus on complex professional tasks and autonomous AI agents. The Chinese tech titan teased the new Qwen4 family last week, taking to X to promise improvements in coding, reasoning and real-world knowledge, while initially making Qwen4-Max available in preview through several of its products. Now, the company has formally detailed the model’s capabilities, pitching it as an always-available “AI teammate” capable of tackling everything from software development to scientific research. 📢 Meet Qwen4-Max, your new AI teammate for work, creativity, and discovery! Qwen4-Max is built on a new MoE architecture with native vision and a 1M-token context window. Highlights: – Outperforms Qwen3.8-Max with up to ~50% fewer tokens, while average cost per task drops over… pic.twitter.com/2Rlkoc6Dm3 — Qwen (@Alibaba_Qwen) November 16, 2026 However, Alibaba appears to be keeping its most powerful model proprietary, despite the open-weight releases that have helped establish Qwen as a major force in the AI realm. Under the hood of Qwen4-Max In a blog post published on Monday, Alibaba revealed that Qwen4-Max is built on a new mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture comprising 2.4 trillion backbone parameters, with 71 billion activated for each token. It also includes another 328 billion parameters dedicated to a technique called “N-gram Embedding,” which helps the model process patterns in text more efficiently. The model supports images as well as text, and comes with a one-million-token context window, allowing it to process large amounts of information in a single interaction. Qwen4-Max is available through Alibaba’s QwenCloud platform, with API pricing starting at $1.50 per million input tokens and $4.50 per million output tokens. It can also be accessed through QwenWork, Qoder and QwenStudio, while Vercel has added Qwen4-Max to its AI Gateway, allowing developers to use the model through coding tools such as Claude Code, Codex and Cursor. Alibaba claims the new architecture delivers substantial improvements over its predecessor, Qwen3.8-Max, particularly when performing complex tasks involving multiple tools and extended periods of autonomous execution. On Work360 , an internal benchmark developed to assess professional tasks across hundreds of specialised fields, Qwen4-Max scored 52.69 compared with 47.74 for Qwen3.8-Max. Alibaba also claims the newer model uses between 24% and 35% fewer tokens on that benchmark, depending on the reasoning effort selected. The company reports even greater token savings on Terminal-Bench 4.0, a test of AI agents’ ability to carry out tasks in a terminal environment, where token usage fell by nearly half compared with Qwen3.8-Max. Alibaba says those improvements, combined with lower API prices, reduced the average cost of completing a task in its Work360 evaluation by 62%, from $4.43 to $1.67. Of course, those are Alibaba’s own results. Independent testing by Artificial Analysis offers another perspective, awarding Qwen4-Max a score of 43 on its Intelligence Index, placing it 38th among 81 models in the comparison. That puts it slightly above the median score of 41 for models in its price category, but lagging leading competitors such as Anthropic’s Claude Fable 5.2 (65), Google’s Gemini 4 Carbon (60) and OpenAI’s GPT-6 Astra (57). Artificial Analysis also calculated an average cost of $3.27 per task across its evaluations, while noting that Qwen4-Max generated 127 million output tokens, considerably more than the median of 78.6 million among comparable models. Caption: Qwen4-Max scores 43 at $3.27 per task. Alibaba pulls its weight(s) The proprietary nature of Qwen4-Max is particularly notable given Alibaba’s recent history. articles.title: Amazon picks its Bond: Robert Pattinson to play 007, ending years of speculation over coveted role
articles.content: Robert Pattinson is taking on the role of 007 in the James Bond film franchise. (Amazon MGM Studios Photo) Last year, Jeff Bezos asked social media , “Who’d you pick as the next Bond?” Amazon now has its own answer: Robert Pattinson. The 40-year-old Pattinson — best known for “Twilight,” “The Batman” and this summer’s “The Odyssey” — becomes the seventh actor to play 007 in the official film series. He takes over from Daniel Craig, whose fifth and last Bond film, “No Time to Die,” came out in 2021. Amazon got a 50% stake in the Bond films when it bought MGM for $8.5 billion in 2022, and it took creative control last year in a joint venture with longtime producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G. Wilson. Fans and bookmakers had been guessing about Craig’s successor since he said in 2019 he was leaving the role. Over the years, the rumored contenders included Idris Elba, Tom Hardy, Aaron Taylor-Johnson, Tom Holland and Henry Cavill. By the end, there were five finalists. Pattinson beat out Nicholas Hoult, Jack Lowden, Josh O’Connor and Callum Turner after screen tests in London in late October, according to The New York Times . Casting director Nina Gold ran the tests, which covered stunts, dialogue and camera presence. Bond is one of the most valuable properties Amazon got in the MGM deal, its second-largest acquisition ever behind Whole Foods. The franchise has earned nearly $7 billion at the domestic box office, adjusted for inflation, since “Dr. No” in 1962. Now Amazon is running it without the Broccoli family, whose stewardship over six decades built it into one of Hollywood’s biggest moneymakers. Pattinson’s casting is the most visible move yet in Amazon’s plans for Bond. As the Times noted, the 2025 deal followed years of behind-the-scenes friction over Amazon’s ambitions to expand the Bond universe beyond the films. The Times also pointed out that Amazon has to win over a generation of moviegoers who grew up during the franchise’s long hiatus and gravitated toward superheroes, horror movies and video game adaptations. Amazon is already putting the back catalog to work. Alongside Monday’s announcement, it published a guide to streaming the 007 films on Prime Video. Identity Confirmed pic.twitter.com/FCU5A9c1wk — James Bond (@007) November 16, 2026 To lead the next film, Amazon brought in producers Amy Pascal, the former Sony Pictures chairwoman, and David Heyman, who produced all eight “Harry Potter” movies. Denis Villeneuve (“Dune”) is directing from an original screenplay by “Peaky Blinders” creator Steven Knight. No release date has been set, and the Times reports that a theatrical release before 2028 is unlikely. “Today marks a defining moment for our studio and a significant milestone in the history of James Bond,” Mike Hopkins, head of Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios, said in a statement . Hopkins said Pattinson’s “remarkable range, magnetic screen presence, and quiet intensity make him an exceptional choice” to carry on the 007 legacy. “James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honor of a lifetime,” Pattinson said. “To say this role is a dream come true is an understatement.” Some longtime fans have worried that under Amazon, Bond will lose his distinctly British character and become more corporate and American, the Times reported. Pascal and Heyman, in a joint statement, called the English actor “the perfect Bond for our times.” Bezos had yet to weigh back in on social media about Amazon’s pick, but Amazon CEO Andy Jassy did in a LinkedIn post , writing that he was “excited” to have Pattinson in the role, calling him “one of the most versatile actors of his generation, who consistently makes fearless choices, and keeps surprising people with his performances.” Fans online were split. Some posted images of Elba or Cavill, calling Pattinson as 007 a “huge miss.” Others said the actor was on a “generational run” right now with the roles…

articles.title: How to Add Native Cross-Chain Swaps to a Wallet or App
articles.content: A practical guide to THORChain integration, quotes, user custody, affiliate fees and reliable swap tracking For a multichain wallet, adding native cross-chain swaps is more than showing a conversion rate. Developers must obtain executable quotes, construct secure source-chain transactions, disclose fees, validate destinations and track settlement across two networks. Integrating an established decentralized exchange (DEX) can provide these capabilities without building independent cross-chain liquidity infrastructure. THORChain is a decentralized cross-chain exchange (DEX) that enables swaps between supported native assets, including bitcoin (BTC) and ether (ETH). A wallet can request a quote, prepare a signed deposit from the user's wallet and monitor the outbound transfer. Users do not need to acquire RUNE separately for a standard supported BTC-to-ETH swap, although the network uses RUNE-paired liquidity internally. Integrators may configure affiliate fees for eligible transactions. Why integrate native cross-chain swaps into a wallet? A user holding assets on multiple blockchains may otherwise move funds through a centralized exchange: deposit an asset, trade it, then withdraw to a different network. An in-wallet swap can reduce that friction and keep the transfer experience in the same product. For developers, however, the feature introduces new responsibilities around quoting, network support, transaction signing, status updates, failed transactions and refunds. Native swaps deliver the actual destination-chain asset, rather than necessarily leaving the user with a wrapped representation. That can be valuable for users converting BTC into native ETH. But a native swap still depends on the settlement network while funds are moving; it is not the same as an instantaneous, risk-free transfer. What are the main ways to integrate THORChain? Integration options at a glance Direct network integration: public quote and status endpoints, no hosted partner key, maximum signing and routing control, and more implementation responsibility. Hosted aggregator API: partner x-api-key, managed eligible routes and fee configuration. Embeddable widget: partner setup and a ready-made swap interface. Third-party SDK: requirements vary by library, underlying route provider and version. 1. Direct integration with THORChain Developers can connect directly to THORChain's public quote and network-status interfaces without a hosted aggregator partner key. Their application must obtain a fresh quote, use the returned current inbound vault address and memo, construct the correct source-chain transaction and reconcile settlement status. Direct integration gives more control but leaves chain-specific signing, monitoring and recovery to the developer. 2. Hosted aggregator API and embeddable widget THORChain Swap offers a hosted aggregator , partner tooling and an embeddable widget. The aggregator at api.thorchain.org/v1 is separate from THORChain's public network interfaces: it requires an x-api-key issued through the affiliate program after review. Approved partners can configure relevant affiliate and service-fee arrangements, request available routes and review earnings. The widget can reduce interface development, but teams still need to test signing, availability, error handling and user support. THORChain's Q3 2026 marketing update describes a hosted routing approach that prioritizes THORChain and may use Maya as an alternative where supported. Available providers and quotes can change; developers should verify the actual route, fees, network state and expected output instead of assuming that a listed option is executable or offers the best price. 3. Third-party SDKs and aggregators SDKs and routing tools such as SwapKit may combine wallet handling with THORChain and other liquidity sources. They can reduce the amount of chain-specific work required, but teams should examine the exact supported providers, versions, API requirements and…

articles.title: Get answers from tables with tabular search in Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base
articles.content: Amazon Bedrock Managed Knowledge Base now supports tabular search, so you can get answers from tables through agentic retrieval. When a question needs data from CSV, XLSX, or XLS files, tabular search looks up values and runs calculations across every relevant row in one or more tables or sheets. It then combines the results with facts from related documents to answer analytical questions that take several steps. A finance team closing the quarter needs to know “Which departments must write variance commentary?” No single file has the answer. It depends on the variance policy’s threshold, the quarter-close memo’s budget revisions, and math over every department in the profit and loss (P&L) workbook. Like this finance team, most teams keep their narratives and data in the same place. For example, a Microsoft SharePoint site holds workbooks next to policies, and an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket holds CSV exports next to PDFs. Tabular search answers questions across these files through the same AgenticRetrieveStream request you already use for documents. It runs code over the original file in an isolated sandbox, so the answer uses the whole table instead of only the rows that retrieval returns. For the finance team, one request returns the departments that must write commentary. The answer cites the policy and the memo, and the trace names the workbook the code read. In this post, you learn how tabular search answers questions that need both table data and facts from documents, and when another tool is a better fit. You also build a knowledge base with sample finance files and use the trace to see which file the code read. Why tables are hard for retrieval Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) returns a fixed number of passages that best match a question, which works well for prose. Tables lose information when they’re split into passages, in ways that depend on the table’s shape: Long tables – A table with thousands of rows spans many passages, and retrieval returns only the few that best match the question. An answer built from them uses a handful of rows, so a total, a comparison, or a threshold check can be incomplete. Wide tables – In a table with hundreds of columns, one row can hold more text than a passage or a search model takes in at once. As a result, values in later columns are harder to match. Long passages from wide tables can also match many unrelated questions and push more relevant passages out of the results. Retrieval also has to match a question to the right table. Questions use business terms, such as “controllable spend,” but tables hold cost center codes, account names, and numbers. A draft and a final workbook look almost the same to search. The rule that gives the numbers meaning is often in a separate document, such as a policy. Tabular search therefore splits the work. Retrieval only has to return one passage from the right table file, and code then reads the whole table. Because retrieval still has to find that file first, naming the file in your question helps. Table 1 shows how plain retrieval and tabular search each handle the finance team’s question, “Which departments must write variance commentary?” Compared Retrieve only Agentic retrieval with tabular search What you get back Passages from the policy, memo, business review, and workbook, but no complete answer An answer naming Sales, Engineering, and Operations, with each department’s variance against its revised budget Revised variance percentages Not available. No file stores them, so no passage can contain them Calculated from every department row in the final workbook Sources Each passage links to its own file, but none of them contains the answer Citations to the finance policy and the close memo. The trace names the workbook the code read Table 1: The same question with plain retrieval and with tabular search. articles.title: Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it
articles.content: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors. For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses. AI changes that. Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment. We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe. But the more freedom we give AI, the harder it becomes to provide the predictability on which trust has traditionally been built. We will not make AI trustworthy by predicting what it will do. We will do it by fencing it in with hard limits that are enforced outside its reach. In OpenAI’s case, the safeguards sat inside a system the agents could edit. But a fence the agents can simply move is not a fence. Where traditional definitions of trust fall short Recent MIT Technology Review coverage has approached this problem from other directions. One contributor argues that having a human in the loop is an insufficient solution because humans are fundamentally unable to understand AI systems’ intentions and advocates instead for interdisciplinary research and collaboration between academia, government, and the tech industry. And a story on reverse game theory describes using incentives to keep models from deviating from the rules, even when no one understands how they work on the inside. Both articles acknowledge that we cannot understand or watch every AI decision. Our instruments of trust, including requirements, testing, certification, safety margins, interlocks, and pass/fail criteria, all depend on our ability to bound a system’s behavior. This is the determinism paradox. With generative and agentic AI, behavior is shaped by training data, architecture, prompts, context, retrieval sources, and the environment. Inputs change, models are updated, tools change, and agents interact. Small variations propagate into outcomes nobody designed. The problem is not randomness; it is that the space of possible behavior is too large to enumerate in advance. Trust must therefore be engineered around boundaries rather than predicted outputs. The goal is not deterministic AI, but bounded, observable, and controllable AI. Trust also cannot be a one-time test. Traditional assurance certifies a product at a point in time, but AI keeps evolving after deployment, and a system that has passed every test can drift outside the conditions that made those tests meaningful. Trust must be continuously earned. Safety engineering has been accounting for some of this variability for decades. For example, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission determine the likelihood of failures in complex systems, and Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP) showed that accidents can emerge from interactions among working components, people, and organizations. But AI raises the stakes, because just a single component can now interpret, infer, and act. The stakes rise further as AI moves from browsers into vehicles, robots, medical systems, industrial controls, and data centers, where a wrong answer can become a life-threatening event. Building trust that scales It’s clear that a person rubber-stamping thousands of AI actions an hour is not an acceptable—or scalable—safeguard against risk. But the remedy is not to remove people from the loop; it is to put human judgment where it counts: setting limits in advance and approving the rare actions that have serious consequences while hard constraints…

articles.title: What Is an Audio Codec? From MP3 to the Tokens Behind AI Music
articles.content: Sampling, bit depth, lossless prediction, auditory masking and MP3, each worked by hand and then measured, and this is still not enough for a model that has to write the music itself. One second of CD audio is 88,200 numbers. A three-minute song is 15,876,000 of them. A language model writing a long essay produces a few thousand tokens. If we asked the same kind of model to write a song one audio sample at a time, it would have to stay coherent over a sequence thousands of times longer than anything it writes in text, and a single wrong number would be audible as a click. Every AI music generator gets around this in the same way. It never touches raw audio. It works on a compressed version, produced by a component called a codec , and most of what these systems can and cannot do follows from how that compression works. This is the first article in my guide to how AI music generators work, and it starts at the bottom of the stack. I will define each term when it first appears, work each idea with numbers small enough to check by hand, then measure it on real audio. The scripts behind every measurement are linked at the end. 1. Sound as numbers: sampling Sound is air pressure changing over time. A microphone turns that pressure into a voltage. To store it, we measure the voltage at regular intervals and write each measurement down. Each measurement is a sample . The number of samples per second is the sample rate , in hertz (Hz, “per second”). How many samples are enough? A pure tone is a wave that repeats. Its frequency is the number of repetitions per second, which we hear as pitch. The sampling theorem (Shannon, 1949 [1]) says: to capture a tone, you need more than two samples per repetition. Put the other way round, a sample rate of R can represent frequencies up to R/2 and nothing above. R/2 is called the Nyquist frequency . Human hearing reaches about 20,000 Hz in young ears. A CD samples 44,100 times per second, so it can represent everything up to 22,050 Hz. What happens to a tone above the limit is instructive. It does not vanish. It comes back as a different, lower tone, an effect called aliasing . A tone at frequency f above the limit shows up at R − f. I generated a 30,000 Hz tone, inaudible to anyone, sampled it at 44,100 Hz, and looked for the strongest frequency in the result: 44,100 − 30,000 = 14,100 Hz (measured: 14,100 Hz) An ultrasonic tone has turned into a clearly audible whistle. This is why every recording device removes everything above the Nyquist frequency before sampling, and why CD’s rate leaves a margin above 20,000 Hz: the filter that does the removing needs room to work. 2. Bit depth and quantization noise Each sample must be stored with finite precision. The bit depth is the number of bits used per sample. With b bits you can write 2ᵇ different values, so every measurement is rounded to the nearest of 2ᵇ levels. A CD uses 16 bits, 65,536 levels. Rounding introduces an error. Over thousands of samples that error behaves like a faint hiss added to the signal, called quantization noise . This idea carries the rest of the article, so it is worth making concrete. The usual measure is the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR): the energy of the signal divided by the energy of the noise. It is expressed in decibels (dB), which are 10 × log₁₀ of an energy ratio. 10 dB means ten times the energy, 20 dB a hundred times, 60 dB a million times. I rounded a full-volume tone to different bit depths and measured the SNR: The rule in the last column is a textbook result and the measurement matches it. The part to remember is the slope. Every bit you add pushes the noise down by 6 dB. Every bit you remove lets it rise by 6 dB. The code for this experiment is three lines: import numpy as np def quantize(x, bits): # x between -1 and 1 levels = 2 ** (bits - 1) - 1 return np.round(x * levels) / levels 3. articles.title: Lambda Boosts AI Factory Resiliency and Efficiency With NVIDIA Photonics
articles.content: To train an AI model, thousands of GPUs have to work together, requiring a network that’s fast, efficient and resilient. Lambda is tackling the network piece of the puzzle with NVIDIA Photonics co-packaged optics (CPO) switches. The cloud provider is using the switches to connect NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 racks with more than 10,000 GPUs, delivering lower power, higher resiliency and longer mean time between interruptions (MTBI) to an AI factory at scale. “Networking has to keep pace with the demands of increasingly large AI clusters,” said Dave Ward, president of cloud services at Lambda. “Bringing co-packaged optics into a deployment of this scale is an important step toward building the infrastructure needed to support the next generation of AI.” Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26 In the company’s tests using the switches, network latency — the time needed for moving data — dropped by about 4% at rack scale and by up to about 10% at pod scale. Across rack, scalable unit and pod configurations, the network maintains the same throughput as conventional pluggable optics. Delivering Power Efficiency and Resiliency at Scale Improving power efficiency and resiliency matters because the network sits at the center of AI factory productivity. In a large training job, one interrupted link can stall thousands of GPUs. With agentic inference, one network disruption can introduce cascading latency effects on many agents. Every interruption costs time, and every watt spent on networking is a watt not available for compute. NVIDIA Photonics addresses both power efficiency and resiliency. By replacing pluggable transceivers with co-packaged optical engines on the switch package, it delivers up to 5x better power efficiency and up to 15x higher reliability than conventional pluggable optics. It also uses 4x fewer lasers, which means fewer components that can fail. Cooler Optics, Replaceable Light Sources Increase Resiliency Lambda’s deployment uses NVIDIA Photonics switches, each with 144 ports running at 800Gb/s. Liquid cooling carries heat away from the switch chip and optical engines. The company reports a median optics temperature of 36°C, compared with 51°C for conventional pluggable optics, and its tests find more stable signal integrity. NVIDIA Photonics also brings the electrical-to-optical conversion closer to the switch chip. Each switch has 18 removable external light sources, which supply light to the optical engines. Optical engines sit alongside the chip on the same package and convert electrical signals into light that carries data over fiber between parts of the cluster. Technicians can replace the light-source modules in the field, unlike traditional pluggable optics, which require replacing the entire module if a laser fails. Co-packaging shortens the electrical path from inches to millimeters, which reduces signal loss. It also removes the need for retimer chips, cutting both power draw and the number of parts in the signal path. Explore NVIDIA Photonics and read Lambda’s deployment announcement . articles.title: NVIDIA Expands Slurm to Bring Quantum Computing Into Supercomputing
articles.content: Quantum processor deployments at supercomputing centers have grown nearly sevenfold over the past five years, with nearly 30 supercomputing centers around the world now in the process of deploying over 50 quantum processors. Many of these centers use Slurm to run scientific supercomputing workloads, so expanding its support for quantum processors builds on familiar workflows and tools, enabling computational chemists, nuclear physicists and materials scientists to bring quantum computing into their research domains without friction. In a new release, Slurm builds on previous work with IBM, Pasqal and the wider quantum computing community to allow QPU builders to create a single interface to their hardware for every supercomputing center, through a simple file. This makes it easier than ever for HPC centers and QPU builders to integrate and serve their hardware. The expansion is already being adopted by Alice & Bob , IBM , IQM , Pasqal , Quantinuum and MQSC and supports the widely used QRMI and QDMI interfaces. Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26 Beating the Bottleneck Until now, integrating a QPU into a supercomputing center meant a new software challenge for every new QPU or supercomputing center. By building on existing quantum-HPC interfaces such as QRMI and QDMI, the Slurm expansion allows QPU builders to reuse their integrations across all their deployments. It also means that supercomputing centers can add new quantum processors to their existing scheduling and resource-management workflows without developing bespoke QPU-specific solutions. For quantum computing to advance science, it needs to be used by scientists. Now scientists can run quantum-classical applications developed with platforms such as NVIDIA CUDA-Q with Slurm coordinating access to all the processing they need. Slurm 26.11 will be available later this month. Orchestrating Resources in an Open Quantum-GPU Platform The Slurm expansion adds a community-developed orchestration layer to NVIDIA’s open platform for quantum-GPU supercomputing, which centers around the CUDA-Q open platform for hybrid quantum-classical computing. At SC26, new releases expand all aspects of the platform: CUDA-Q QEC allows researchers developing quantum error correction to rapidly prototype and test new ideas, including with a new decoder server . A new TCBP-JOBS decoder is 13,000x faster than the industry standard. CUDA-Q gets an expanded layer of fault-tolerant primitives that application builders can use to realistically compile their ideas. Fermilab has already used CUDA-Q to perform studies in three weeks that would normally have taken five months. CUDA-Q Algorithms provides reusable components for builders of quantum applications, including new capabilities in helping design the loading data into quantum circuits and tools specifically for chemistry and materials applications CUDA-Q Pulse gives quantum hardware builders a layer for shaping the ‘pulses’ needed to control qubits on a QPU, including tools to GPU accelerate their generation. The quantum ecosystem around the world is continuing to build with this platform. Quantum Motion integrated its QUICHE chemistry framework with CUDA-Q. Altera and Oxford Quantum Circuits designed an FPGA-based controller connecting qubit control and readout to GPUs through NVQLink. At supercomputing scale, QunaSys used cuQuantum and 1,024 NVIDIA Hopper GPUs on ABCI-Q to simulate more than 300 million quantum operations, reaching chemical accuracy for a four-hydrogen-atom model. NVIDIA researchers used JUPITER to simulate 104 qubits under realistic noise, testing fault-tolerant designs before they’re built. Learn more about NVIDIA quantum computing technologies . articles.title: NVIDIA Sweeps MLPerf Training and Endpoints as Vera Rubin Debuts With Leading Performance
articles.content: In its MLPerf benchmarks debut, with results released today, the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform delivers leading performance across training, post-training and agentic inference. NVIDIA swept every MLPerf Training v6.1 benchmark and, in its first MLPerf Endpoints submission, delivered more than 10x generational gains in throughput per watt for agentic AI — measuring how much agentic work a system delivers with each watt of power. These results are just the beginning. Vera Rubin performance will keep climbing through continuous optimization of NVIDIA’s CUDA-powered software stack , so the infrastructure that customers invest in today delivers more value over time. NVIDIA Sweeps MLPerf Training v6.1 AI agents are now everywhere, writing code, running business workflows, answering customer questions and, as this week’s SC26 conference highlights , advancing scientific research. Faster training means smarter agents can reach users sooner, drug discovery models can keep pace with new lab data and fraud-detection models can adapt to new threats faster. MLPerf Training measures how fast a system can train a range of AI models to a target level of accuracy. The NVIDIA platform was the only one with results on every benchmark this round, spanning large language models, image generation, recommender systems and reinforcement learning post-training. In its debut, Vera Rubin NVL72 delivered up to 2x more performance per GPU than the highly optimized NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 system — early results that show the pace of generation-over-generation innovation. MLPerfTraining v6.1 results retrieved from www.mlcommons.org on Nov 16, 2026, from the following entries: 6.1-0116 , 6.1-0030, 6.1-0135, 6.1-0020, 6.1-0049, 6.1-0123, 6.1-0138, 6.1-0073, 6.1-0124, 6.1-0129 and 6.1-0038. The MLPerf name and logo are trademarks of MLCommons Association in the United States and other countries. All rights reserved. Unauthorized use is strictly prohibited. See www.mlcommons.org for more information. NVIDIA also demonstrated performance at scale. On the DeepSeek-V3 benchmark, Vera Rubin NVL72 scaled from 256 to 1,024 GPUs with about 97% efficiency: quadrupling the GPUs cut time to train from 16 minutes to about four. NVIDIA also ran the benchmark on 10,240 GPUs with GB300 systems, representing the largest scale in this round. Microsoft Azure matched that scale with 10,240 NVIDIA GPUs with GB200 systems. Results at this scale matter because adding GPUs only speeds up training if they can work together efficiently. NVIDIA NVLink scale-up networking connects the GPUs within each system so they act as one, while NVIDIA Quantum-X800 InfiniBand and Spectrum-X Ethernet scale-out networking link those systems across the data center. Combined with optimized software, this keeps thousands of GPUs working in concert, helping developers build more intelligent models while cutting training times. NVIDIA Vera Rubin Leads Agentic Inference on MLPerf Endpoints An AI agent for travel that plans and books a whole trip — or an IT agent that finds and fixes a problem before anyone files a ticket — may reason, call tools and check its work many times to finish a single task. Each of those steps generates tokens. Because AI data centers are limited by power, the more tokens a system can generate each second for every watt of power, the more agents it can serve and the more value it creates. MLPerf Endpoints tests systems on real agentic coding and enterprise workflows, and checks that the agents still complete their tasks correctly. NVIDIA Vera Rubin leads across all of its agentic benchmarks. For example, in a provisional result for Kimi K3, a large open model built for agentic workflows, Vera Rubin NVL72 systems deliver more than 10x the throughput per watt of NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 at the same response speed. articles.title: NVIDIA CUDA-X Libraries Give Agents the Tools to Accelerate Scientific Discovery
articles.content: With expanded NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, including cuPhoton, cuPotential and cuSpa, researchers can sift through vast amounts of data to accelerate research, from astrophysics and materials science to single-cell biology. The speedups are helping scientists analyze larger datasets and model more complex systems. The new libraries give AI agents the tools to help researchers make discoveries faster than ever. Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26 Bringing Black Holes Into Focus Seeing a black hole takes a telescope the size of Earth. The Event Horizon Telescope links radio dishes worldwide, generating petabytes of data that can take months to process. With NVIDIA cuPhoton.xBeam, a module within the cuPhoton Toolkit , black hole observations from the Event Horizon Telescope can now be correlated orders of magnitude faster than ever. Analysis that once took over a month now takes eight minutes. By combining global radio dishes into Earth-sized aperture, cuPhoton delivers unprecedented astronomical imaging resolution. cuPhoton successfully correlated observations of powerful black hole jets J1924 and 3C279 in the night sky — making it a reality to reconstruct a Messier 87* black hole galaxy in real time. The entire pipeline, from data loading and processing to visualization, runs on distributed multi-GPU systems or a compact NVIDIA DGX Spark system, helping scientists study how gas spirals inward under a black hole’s powerful gravitational pull. Steering Fusion Simulations Sustaining plasma at millions of degrees is essential to achieving stable, continuous fusion energy. But simulating its behavior is costly: on petascale systems, a single time step can take days, with simulations running for weeks. Experiments also generate data faster than traditional pipelines can process it, often leaving scientists waiting until experiments end to analyze results. Pacific Fusion researchers used NVIDIA cuPhoton.xLens module to extract insights while plasma simulations run, helping them visualize what’s happening as results emerge. The NVIDIA cuPhoton.xLens module extracts insights while plasma simulations run, helping researchers understand what’s happening as results emerge. Researchers can couple the entire pipeline with an NVIDIA Nemotron -powered agent running locally on the same system, enabling interactive analysis that can help steer simulations in real time to inform fusion reactor target and chamber design. Exploring Potential Medicines Molecular simulations help scientists evaluate drug designs before costly laboratory experiments. NVIDIA cuPotential, built on work by researchers at Simons Foundation’s Flatiron Institute and D. E. Shaw Research , accelerates existing simulation software by up to 3x while improving calculation stability and accuracy. It expedites synthetic data creation for generative AI models, finding previously unknown molecular binding sites and calculating the strength of molecular interactions. NVIDIA is working with Schrödinger and the AMBER , NAMD , GROMACS , LAMMPS and Open Molecular Software Foundation communities to bring cuPotential acceleration to molecular dynamics engines and workflows. Cadence , Fathom Therapeutics , Topos Bio , Genesis Molecular AI and Terray Therapeutics are adopting it for drug discovery. Accelerating Materials Research Daviator , a collection of batched GPU kernels for the widely used Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package, is coming to NVIDIA ALCHEMI — delivering quantum-mechanical calculations up to 22x faster and at up to 75% lower cost. With Daviator, researchers building simulation models can now use GPU acceleration across atomistic systems of all sizes to generate the millions of calculations of atomic interactions needed for model training and inference, including for small systems that previously ran faster on CPUs. articles.title: CUDA at 20: How the Platform Transformed Scientific Computing
articles.content: This week at SC26, NVIDIA is marking two decades of CUDA by honoring the researchers, developers and engineers who helped make GPU computing a foundation for modern science and AI. CUDA’s 20th anniversary presents an occasion to reflect across computing eras, from the people who wrote the very first CUDA programs to the AI developers building on their work today. At the platform’s core is this developer community whose experiments, tools and persistence expanded what accelerated computing could do. From SC06 to SC26 NVIDIA announced CUDA in November 2006 and brought it to the scientific community at SC06, giving scientists and developers a familiar, high-level programming model for using GPUs. It fundamentally extended accelerated computing beyond graphics use cases to accelerate demanding applications for science, simulation and more. In the two decades since, developers have used CUDA to advance Nobel Prize-winning AI research , accelerate scientific applications on supercomputers and support visual effects in Oscar-winning films . Today, more than 11 million developers build on CUDA across the computing stack. Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26 Honoring the Architects of Progress Now, at SC26, NVIDIA is looking back at some of the CUDA luminaries who’ve spearheaded breakthroughs in science and AI: At the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, biophysicist Klaus Schulten’s team helped connect GPU computing with molecular biology through Nanoscale Molecular Dynamics and Visual Molecular Dynamics , tools for molecular simulation and visualization. In 2013, researchers at Illinois, the University of Pittsburgh and Vanderbilt University used CUDA-accelerated tools to help resolve the HIV capsid’s atomic structure. They combined experiments with simulations on Blue Waters , one of the world’s most powerful supercomputers at the time. In a critical breakthrough in AI, University of Toronto researchers Alex Krizhevsky, Ilya Sutskever and Geoffrey Hinton used CUDA to train AlexNet on just two NVIDIA GPUs. Their image-recognition system won the 2012 ImageNet competition , helping demonstrate the potential of GPU computing for deep learning. That connection between computing and scientific discovery is seen with AlphaFold, which predicts protein structures. Demis Hassabis and John Jumper shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry for protein structure prediction. Their team’s publicly released AlphaFold 2 software uses CUDA for GPU execution . These are just a few of many examples that show how one generation’s work creates opportunities for the next. With 1,000+ NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries, developers are now reshaping industries and giving machines the power to see, learn and reason — from discovering new medicines and designing next-generation factories to advancing autonomous vehicles, modeling financial markets and unlocking quantum computing — and more. Start building with the CUDA Toolkit and visit the 20-Year CUDA Celebration Event Wall at NVIDIA’s booth at SC26 . Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26

articles.title: NVIDIA Announces Rubin HPC — A New GPU to Accelerate Agents for Science, Engineering and Analytics
articles.content: Announced today at SC26, NVIDIA Rubin HPC is a new GPU in the NVIDIA Vera Rubin platform designed to accelerate simulation and data processing for science, engineering and analytics workflows. As agents help scientists and engineers explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs, they rely on simulations to test those ideas and guide their next steps. Rubin HPC will accelerate those simulations, shortening the path from exploration to scientific discovery and industrial design. The Rubin HPC GPU features a record number of CUDA cores — more than 50,000 on a single GPU — as well as a sparse data acceleration capability that keeps those cores fed with data, and accelerates GPU-to-GPU connectivity with seventh-generation NVIDIA NVLink interconnect technology. Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26 Scientists and engineers rely on simulation to understand complex systems before committing to experiments or physical prototypes. Working with agents, these teams can explore more candidate materials, molecules and designs. This increases demand for the GPU-accelerated simulations needed to evaluate those ideas and guide next steps. “For agents tackling science and engineering, faster simulation means faster discovery,” said Ian Buck , vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing at NVIDIA. “Rubin HPC accelerates the simulations agents use to test ideas and guide their next steps, helping scientists and engineers explore more possibilities and bring breakthroughs closer.” Turning Faster Computation Into Faster Discovery Across climate models, engineering simulations, genomic analysis and financial risk, scientific computing workloads take a similar shape: an application reaches into an immense dataset, gathers a handful of scattered values, calculates a result and repeats this on an enormous scale. To help address the challenge, Rubin HPC will offer a balanced design, scaling data movement and compute together rather than increasing compute alone. That balance is what optimizes Rubin HPC for scientific computing. It keeps the GPU’s record number of CUDA cores supplied with data, so they spend their time computing rather than waiting. This accelerates recurring patterns of every simulation workload — from sparse matrix operations to stencil computations to sorting and reductions. These patterns are prevalent across data analytics, science and engineering workloads, which is why a purpose-built GPU delivering the broadest acceleration can help unlock cross-industry breakthroughs. NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries offer a growing set of optimized implementations of complex algorithms for agents to use, including those most relevant to simulation and analytics. Used together with Rubin HPC, the libraries can give agents the fastest glide path to reasoning outcomes. And faster agent-invoked simulations mean faster feedback — shortening the loop of hypothesis, simulation and refinement, so researchers and engineers can choose next steps sooner and point lab work at the most promising candidates. Rubin HPC is expected to be available in 2028. Read All NVIDIA Announcements From SC26

articles.title: Every Film Starts as a Poster
articles.content: I built an open-source Claude Code plugin that turns a sentence into a flat illustration, then opens it into a 3D world with a moving camera One sentence in, this film out. No photo, no 3D model, no image generator, nothing drawn by hand. Watch the first second of the film above. It looks like a printed poster: a flat illustration of a village under the mountains. Then the camera moves, and the poster turns out to be a place. You fly down a lane between the chalets, over the ski slope, past the gondola and into the square. Then the camera pulls back, the world flattens, and you are looking at the poster again. The loop starts over without a seam. That moment, when a flat picture opens into a world, is the whole idea behind Depth Diorama , a plugin I built for Claude Code. You describe a place or a product in one sentence. Claude builds it as a real 3D scene. The engine films it with that poster-to-world camera move. Here is the sentence behind the village: A mountain ski village at night in falling snow: wooden chalets with glowing windows climbing the slope, a gondola lift with cabins gliding up to the peak, skiers coming down a lit piste, a small clock tower and a church spire in the square, string lights across the lane, a frozen pond where people skate, pine trees heavy with snow, and the mountain under a starry sky. About twenty minutes after I gave Claude that sentence, it handed back a film at 60 frames a second . In between, it built the village, reviewed its own frames over eleven rounds of fixes, and rendered only once every automatic check passed. The poster is not a fake The flat picture and the deep world are the same thing. Nothing is swapped and nothing is faked. The same scene. Left: the first frame. Right: three seconds later. It is an old camera trick. Film a scene from very far away through a very long lens, and everything in it, near or far, ends up about the same distance from the camera. Depth disappears, and the scene stacks into one flat picture. Then move the camera in while widening the lens. The subject stays the same size, but the space behind it stretches open. Filmmakers call this a dolly zoom . Depth Diorama does this with a real 3D scene. The poster you see in the first frame really is the 3D world, seen from kilometres away. Claude builds the world, the engine films it The split is simple. Claude is the art director. The engine is the camera crew. 1. Claude writes the world as a small scene file. It is plain JavaScript that builds the place from a kit of parts: buildings, curved shapes, people, lights, snow, drawn pictures for signs and screens, and a camera path. A shortened example: export default { name: "Lantern Street", look: "night", build(k) { k.ground(300, 400, "#2B2D44"); for (let i = 0; i < 6; i++) { const z = -i * 12; k.building(10, 18, 10, [-11, z], { wall: "#4A4D73", lit: "#FFD98A" }); k.building(10, 22, 10, [11, z], { wall: "#5A4C78", lit: "#FFC3A0" }); k.light([0, 4, z], 9, "#FFB060", 1.2); // warm light spilling onto the street } k.crowd(120, { x: [-5, 5], z: [-60, 4], umbrellas: 0.5 }); k.particles({ count: 3000, fall: 2, sway: 2 }); // falling snow }, }; Real scenes run much longer. The ski village is about 860 lines: around 30 chalets, 400 snowy pines and 90 people, a gondola with 18 moving cabins, skiers, skaters, a sleigh and chimney smoke. 2. Claude reviews its own frames, round after round. It renders a still at every key moment of the film and looks at each one. Is anything empty, muddy, clipped or stiff? It names the three weakest things in each frame, fixes them and renders again. The plugin asks for at least six rounds, because a first version always looks empty. Four moments from one film: a rainy neon crossing. 3. The engine checks the film. Before the final render, it tests what a person would miss: PASS Flat shot reads as flat PASS Flat shot fills the frame PASS Every move opens real depth PASS Camera is never inside an object PASS Same time renders the same…

articles.title: Capacity Planning for Kubernetes Ingress Controllers: A Practical Guide
articles.content: Tuning, scaling up vs out, and how much headroom is enough. Scaling up or out, matched to the headroom you already trust. Capacity planning for Kubernetes ingress controllers. Two ways to add capacity, scaling up with fewer larger pods or scaling out with more smaller pods, aimed at the same headroom target and validated with soak and spike tests. In the previous article , Traefik met the performance objectives for our workload, as long as it ran with enough replicas. NGINX still did about twice the work per CPU core. The verdict was “fast enough, if you size it right.” This article is about the “size it right” part. Our real traffic was never the problem. It sat more than 50 times below even the smallest setup I tested. The real question was different: how much Traefik do we need to keep the same safety margin our NGINX setup gave us? Answering it took four steps. Get what’s free from tuning, pick the right way to scale, turn the results into a replica plan, and prove the plan holds over time and under spikes. My example is Traefik replacing NGINX, but the same four steps work for any ingress controller. Start With the Target A capacity plan needs a target, just like a benchmark does. Without one, “enough” turns into whatever number feels safe on the day. Our target was simple: match the headroom of the controller we were replacing. Headroom is the gap between the traffic you expect and the most traffic the system can handle while still healthy. NGINX had been running 5 to 10 pods with 1 CPU core each, and its headroom had served us well. Traefik had to offer about the same. “Healthy” matters here. In the last article, I separated the ceiling , the highest throughput reached while still healthy, from the optimum , the point just below it where latency is still close to its minimum. The capacity numbers in this article are ceilings, taken while errors were zero and latency was still low. Real traffic should then sit near the optimum, well below them. I kept the same method as before. k6, an open-source load-testing tool, sent load straight to the controller pods, swept from a few users up to thousands, and every level ran three times, reported as the median, to smooth out run-to-run noise. The autoscaler was pinned so the pod count couldn’t change mid-run. The setup itself was stronger this time, with a bigger backend behind the controllers, so nothing else could become the limit at higher throughput. Measured side by side again, NGINX came out about 2.2× faster on 1-core pods and 2.1× on 2-core pods, a little less than the 2.4× in the last article. The ratio held, which is why ratios, not absolute numbers, drive the plan. With the target fixed, the first question was whether Traefik could do more with what it already had. Step 1: Tune Before You Scale Tuning is free. Scaling costs CPU every hour of every day. So before adding resources, I looked for configuration changes that let Traefik do more on the same budget. I picked what to test from the symptoms, not from a list of popular tips. In the last article, Traefik’s memory grew under load while its throughput fell, which pointed to the garbage collector competing for CPU. Access logs were the other obvious cost paid on every request. I tried the popular tips too, and they’re covered below. The method matters as much as the result. The baseline was the configuration we actually ran: access logs on, buffered, and no garbage collector tuning. From there, I changed one setting at a time on identical resources, 2 pods with 1 core each, then combined the ones that helped. The winning combination was then confirmed over three trials. Each setting tested alone, then together, on the same 2 pods × 1 core. Confirmed over 3 trials: 4,255 → 6,145 req/s. Two changes made the difference: Access logs off: about 28% more throughput. Traefik ships with access logs off, but many teams turn them on for debugging, as we had. Traefik then writes a log line for every request, and even with…

articles.title: Best practices for writing Denied Topics in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails
articles.content: With Denied Topics in Amazon Bedrock Guardrails , you block a content category by describing it in plain language, and the guardrail applies that description to every request by meaning rather than by keyword. That same mechanism can also match more than you intend. A topic named Finance, meant to keep an assistant out of investment advice, also blocks “When does my direct deposit clear?”. Inputs close in meaning to the topic can get caught, not only the requests you intended. When Denied Topics blocks too much or too little, the cause is usually one of four authoring patterns: Topics that block legitimate queries. A topic framed around a subject domain (Finance, Legal, Compensation) rather than the user’s intention can match queries semantically near that domain. This is a frequent failure mode. Topics that miss the requests they were written to catch. A definition built from keyword lists (“words like invest, portfolio, stock…”) misses phrasings that use other vocabulary and fires on unrelated inputs that happen to share those words. Examples that teach the wrong thing. Five paraphrases of one idea leave the topic’s boundaries unguarded, and examples that name specific countries, products, or companies pull those entities into the topic’s context. Topics that interfere with each other. Overlapping definitions compete for the same input, report matches inconsistently, and can together block inputs that neither would block alone. The rest of this post is a practical guide to avoiding these patterns. It presents eight best practices for describing a topic precisely enough that the guardrail blocks what you mean and passes what you don’t. The scenario: AnyCompany Bank’s customer assistant To ground the following practices in something concrete, we use one running example throughout this post: a fictional bank we call AnyCompany Bank. AnyCompany Bank is two weeks from launching its first customer-facing AI assistant, and its first pass at the Denied Topics policy is blocking the wrong things. Application: AnyCompany Bank’s chatbot is embedded in the AnyCompany Bank mobile and web app. It answers questions about accounts, statements, transfers, cards, and mortgages. It hands off to a human for account changes, dispute filings, and questions outside its scope. Must-block list (from legal and compliance): Personalized investment recommendations (a regulatory line, because AnyCompany Bank isn’t registered as an investment adviser through this channel). Legal counsel or litigation guidance regarding disputes against AnyCompany Bank. Insider-trading advice (a specific slice of financial advice with its own regulatory weight). Descriptions of how to build weapons (universal safety, not domain-specific). Prompt injection or jailbreak attempts (a different kind of signal, because the request is trying to override the assistant’s own instructions). Repeating specific named competitor products in AnyCompany Bank’s outputs. Must-pass list (the things the assistant exists to do): Account balance and statement questions. Transfer instructions, payoff quotes, escrow questions. Card management, fraud reports (routed to a human), lost-card replacement. Mortgage servicing operations, such as modifications, forbearance, and payment plans. General financial-literacy questions (“What is a certificate of deposit?”), phrased as education rather than personalized advice. Against that target, AnyCompany Bank’s team first drafted four topics, all of them currently blocking legitimate queries: Finance → blocks "When does my direct deposit clear?" Legal → blocks "Can you help me modify my mortgage?" Fraud → blocks "My card was skimmed at a gas station, what do I do?" Competitors → blocks any mention of a rival product, including customer questions comparing options Every one of these topics names a subject domain the assistant works in, rather than the intention the bank needs to refuse. Fixing this is what the rest of the post is about. The next eight…
articles.author: Jian Zhang

articles.title: What went wrong with Outlook: Microsoft blames ‘thundering herds’ and a bug unnoticed for months
articles.content: A months-old bug set off last week’s Outlook outage. (GeekWire Illustration / GPT-6.1 Sol) Microsoft’s own safety systems helped turn a dormant software flaw into last week’s global Outlook outage , rerouting traffic from failing servers onto healthy ones that had the same problem, until more than 80% of the servers in its Microsoft 365 networking gateway had stopped responding. That phenomenon, known as a cascading failure, is one of the findings in Microsoft’s preliminary report on the outage, released overnight, dissecting the failure that cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries. Related ‘I hope this email finds you’: Microsoft declares outage over as the world digs out of its inbox According to the report, the attempts to recover were further complicated by a second problem: servers that engineers restarted were immediately overwhelmed by waiting traffic and stopped responding again, a phenomenon known as a “thundering herd.” Microsoft says active service disruptions lasted nearly 24 hours. Delayed email continued to be delivered after service returned Friday morning, and the company posted its public all-clear on X late Friday night, nearly 38 hours after the outage began. The underlying flaw dates to July, when Microsoft began rolling out a fix to the software that handles incoming connections on its networking gateway, the servers that sit in front of Outlook and many other Microsoft 365 services. Microsoft hasn’t said what the fix was meant to address. It ran worldwide for more than three months without problems, according to the report. Under heavy load, however, parts of that software could get stuck waiting on one another, using up the servers’ processing power and memory until they froze. That’s what happened last week. About 15 hours before the outage, Microsoft’s systems automatically moved Teams traffic onto the same servers that handle Outlook email, adding to their load, according to the report. Microsoft called the switch part of normal operations but didn’t say what prompted it. Complicating matters, nearly 14% of the gateway’s server capacity was already out of service because of an unrelated problem, which also isn’t detailed in the report. When traffic peaked during the U.S. workday, that was enough to trigger the outage. Two things stand out as likely areas of scrutiny: Microsoft’s testing didn’t catch the bug. Its labs mostly used less powerful machines with fewer processing cores, running a different mix of traffic, while the problem was worst on the newer servers handling real customer load. The fix also passed through Microsoft’s standard staged rollout, spreading worldwide over several weeks without any sign of trouble, according to the report. The company certainly has the means to test on the hardware it actually runs. It spent $45.2 billion on capital expenditures in its most recent quarter, much of it on AI infrastructure. The safeguards meant to contain the damage didn’t hold . Walls between regions failed because of what the report calls “a separate issue,” which it doesn’t explain, so the outage went global. The gateway is made up of thousands of “capacity units” grouped into regions, with walls between them meant to keep a failure in one place. Microsoft also runs a second, independent gateway so services can switch over during a disruption. Teams, OneDrive, SharePoint and Office apps made that switch, which is why Teams chats and meetings mostly kept working. Exchange couldn’t, “for scale reasons,” as the company put it, so email stayed down. Microsoft’s own tools added to the problem. Its automated recovery “was not designed” for a fleet that was almost entirely unresponsive, according to the report, and its usual ways of rolling back a bad change couldn’t quickly undo one that…

articles.title: What is the FAA’s SMART AI system? Officials are denying a link to the nationwide ground stop
articles.content: The airline ground stop that wreaked havoc on travel since Friday was not related to the FAA’s new, $875 million AI -powered system the agency is rolling out to help predict problems in the sky, according to government officials and the artificial intelligence company behind the technology. But the timing of the ground stop, so close to the national rollout of the Federal Aviation Administration’s SMART system, has raised questions about what the system does, its benefits and risks compared with the existing human system and what guardrails there are to address potential problems. Officials say no connection to ground stop The SMART system is based in a single location near Washington where a team of experts analyzes flight schedules, weather forecasts and hundreds of other streams of data. Then that office sends recommendations to the FAA’s command center, which relays them to air traffic controllers across the country for consideration. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said Friday there’s no indication the communications issues that caused the ground stop are linked to the new computer system, and the top officials at the Transportation Department and FAA reiterated that Saturday. The startup that designed the system, Air Space Intelligence, or ASI, said the ground stop wasn’t caused by “the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC.” But lawmakers and outside groups raised questions about the SMART system before Friday’s ground stop. Last month, House Democrats sent a letter to the U.S. Government Accountability Office requesting an audit of the new software, raising concerns about safety and guardrails. “Concerningly, the nation’s front line aviation safety workforce apparently had little to no input into SMART’s development and have received limited training and information during the current deployment process,” the Oct. 13 letter said. “The use of artificial intelligence within SMART has rightfully raised serious questions about its reliability and safety benefits, particularly on its potential to interfere with decision-making by experienced air traffic controllers or to hallucinate safety-critical information.” SMART, however, is not — at least not yet — set up for AI to be in charge of flight control. Rather, it is making recommendations to humans who do so. What is the SMART system? Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford unveiled the system in September, calling it a “cutting-edge tool that centralizes 200 data streams — including weather patterns, flight paths, traffic flow, and controller staffing metrics — into one platform.” SMART stands for Strategic Management of Airspace, Routes and Trajectories. The system’s AI-supported engine synthesizes the data systems and shows a “comprehensive visualization” of where planes are going, how much traffic the system can handle and where congestion or weather could cause problems, according to the announcement. The idea is for specialists to then use the platform to fix problems before they arise. The FAA says that during the initial test of the system in the Washington area this fall, the system helped reroute 180 flights and saved an average of 10 minutes and 80 gallons of fuel per flight by diverting around weather or other issues. The agency said that one flight cut 42 minutes off its trip from Tampa, Florida, to Dallas thanks to the system’s recommendations. So SMART was expanded for use nationwide on Nov. 10 for the airspace of all 22 air traffic control centers. That was three days before the ground stop. According to a government fact sheet on the tool, SMART can predict where air traffic is headed and identify other routes before an area becomes too congested. The system can also help reopen restricted airspace faster and better manage airport arrivals. SMART is also supposed…

articles.title: 'Slow Horses' to Hit 10-Season Milestone With Apple TV Renewal
articles.content: Apple has renewed its popular British spy drama "Slow Horses" for ninth and tenth seasons, extending its considerable lead as Apple TV 's longest-running original series by season, according to Deadline . Six seasons of Slow Horses have already been released, with seasons seven and eight already confirmed before the latest renewal. The order for seasons nine and ten extends its lead as the ‌Apple TV‌ original with the most seasons commissioned. The commitment puts "Slow Horses" well ahead of other established Apple originals. "For All Mankind," which debuted when the service launched in 2019, will finish with season six . "Slow Horses" has also maintained an exceptional critical reception, with all six seasons holding critics' scores of 95% or higher on Rotten Tomatoes . Seasons two and four have perfect 100% ratings, while the latest season holds 98%. The news answers recent uncertainty about the show's future. Cast member Olivia Cooke had suggested just days earlier that season eight could mark its conclusion. The television series is catching up with the book series it is based on that began 16 years ago. Author Mick Herron has published nine main "Slough House" novels since the first one debuted in 2010, with gaps of between one and three years between installments. The latest, "Clown Town," arrived in 2025, three years after "Bad Actors." Those two books provide the material for seasons seven and eight, raising the possibility that seasons nine and ten could move beyond the published novels. Apple has not confirmed that direction, with a spokesperson telling Deadline that story details for the additional seasons would follow. Produced by See-Saw Films, "Slow Horses" centers on an outpost of MI5 where agents are sent after damaging their professional reputations. Gary Oldman plays their boss, "Jackson Lamb," alongside a cast that includes Jack Lowden, Kristin Scott Thomas, Jonathan Pryce, and Cooke. The first six seasons are available to stream now on ‌Apple TV‌. articles.title: Microsoft is hiking cloud prices in India — but dropping costs in China and other markets
articles.content: Microsoft raising cloud prices for customers in India, New Zealand by 15%, 10% Currency fluctuations have afforded three countries to get cheaper cloud prices Brazil changes also on the cards, Japan announcement expected later Microsoft has confirmed the details of its latest currency adjustments in a bid to keep local pricing more closely aligned with its global pricing levels and to account for exchange rate fluctuations, and it's bad news for India which is set to see cloud pricing increases of 15.7%. New Zealand will also see a 10% rise, while the two nations will also see rises of up to 20% and 10% across on-prem pricing. But not all countries are seeing price hikes – China (-8.5%), Norway (-5.9%) and Australia (-4%) will each see a decrease in cloud pricing in line with currency exchange rates. These three countries see no change to on-prem pricing. Microsoft announces its latest exchange rate-linked pricing adjustments It's worth noting that individual products may see slightly different adjustments based on rounding rules and also how the prices are calculated, but the above percentages offer a preview into the sort of changes customers in these five nations can expect to see in the new year. The company confirmed in a blog post that the changes will come into effect from January 1, 2027, as part of a new scheme it introduced in July 2026 whereby the hyperscaler would adjust prices each January for greater predictability, rather than at random points throughout the year. Microsoft is also looking to adjust its Brazil pricing following the implementation of the nation's tax reform, while Japan will remain on its previous annual April cadence (with an announcement on track for February 2027). It's argues that the revisions will help maintain competitive and regionally consistent prices for its cloud services, but some customers worry that currency fluctuations can make identical services more expensive or cheaper depending on where customers are billed. Crucially though, these adjustments are purely a response to global currency fluctuations, and it's not a sign that Microsoft is raising its prices across the board.

articles.title: Mercedes' clever new driving assist handles complex traffic like a champ
articles.content: Mercedes-Benz provided flights from Washington, DC, to San Francisco, and accommodation so Ars could try its new driver assistance systems. Ars does not accept paid editorial content. SAN FRANCISCO—When Ars first drove the new Mercedes-Benz CLA last year , the automaker also gave us a sneak preview of its next driver assist. Called Drive Assist Pro, it’s for collaborative partially assisted driving, and from the passenger seat at the time, the demo was impressive . Now the automaker is getting ready to start rolling out Drive Assist Pro to customers with cars running the new MB.OS operating system here in the US and in Germany, and it let us have some time behind the wheel. While most automakers want a reputation associated with safety, Mercedes has long used passive and active technology to do so in its products. It was one of the first OEMs to introduce airbags, then a decade later started adding active safety systems like antilock brakes, electronic stability control, and adaptive cruise control. And so, by giving the car’s electronics the ability to control the brakes, and throttle, we arrive at the first level of assisted driving—called “level 1” in automotive engineerspeak. “Level 2” assisted driving, where the car also controls the steering as well as the acceleration and braking, got famous with Tesla Autopilot. But the first lane-keeping assists predate it by almost a decade in passenger cars, when Toyota introduced a system in 2004. The human driver behind the wheel is still in charge, responsible for situational awareness (and anything that arises from a lack thereof), with the idea that long drives become less tiring and a little more effortless when the car does the boring job of keeping a constant speed or a constant distance to the car ahead and between the white lines.
